lead: A shaft spinning at N revolutions per minute and carrying torque T delivers power. The same power can come from a high speed with small torque or a low speed with large torque. Motor shafts, car drive shafts and turbine shafts all use this relation. This chapter gives the power–torque–speed formula, then the design route: find the torque from power and speed, size the shaft for shear strength, and check that it does not twist too much.
prereq: You need: 6.1 for τ = 16T/(πd³) and 6.2 for the twist check.

blocks.text: Power is the rate of doing work. A rotating shaft does work by turning against a torque. If the shaft turns faster, it delivers the same torque more often, so it delivers more power. The link is the angular speed ω, the angle turned per second in radians per second (rad/s). One full turn is 2π rad. A speed of N revolutions per minute is N/60 turns per second, so ω = 2πN/60 rad/s.

blocks.where: P is power in watts (W); T is torque in newton metres (N·m); ω is angular speed in rad/s; N is speed in revolutions per minute (rpm).

blocks.text: If power is given in kilowatts, convert to watts first. In kW form the same equation is P = 2πNT/60000, with P in kW, T in N·m and N in rpm. The factor 60000 comes from 60 seconds per minute and 1000 W per kW.

For a fixed power, torque and speed pull in opposite directions. A 10 kW shaft at 100 rpm carries about 955 N·m. The same 10 kW at 1000 rpm carries only about 95 N·m. Figure 1 shows this curve. Slow shafts are fat because they need high torque; fast shafts can be slender for the same power.

sections.h3: The design route for a shaft

blocks.text: A designer is usually given the power P and the speed N. The job is to find a safe diameter d. Start from the power equation and work towards the stress equation from 6.1.

items: Convert P to watts and N to rad/s: ω = 2πN/60.
For a solid shaft, use τmax = 16T/(πd³). Set τmax equal to the allowable shear stress τallow and solve: d³ = 16T/(πτallow).
Take the cube root to get d, then round up to the next standard shaft size.
Check the twist with 6.2: θ/L = T/(GJ) must be within the allowable value. Use J = πd⁴/32 for a solid shaft.

blocks.text: A hollow shaft is used when saving weight matters, as in aircraft or long line shafts. Its polar second moment of area is J = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32, with D the outer diameter and d the inner diameter. Use τ = Tr/J with r = D/2 at the outer surface. The strength design may give a thin wall, but the stiffness check often decides the final wall thickness. Some syllabi call this power transmission by circular shafts.

sections.h3: Speed, torque and the whole machine

blocks.text: A motor nameplate gives power and speed together: for example, 15 kW at 1440 rpm. The torque at the motor shaft follows from these two numbers. A gearbox or belt drive then changes speed and torque. In an ideal drive the product Tω stays constant, so reducing speed raises torque in the same ratio. Real drives lose a few percent to friction.

The same power can be carried at different speeds, but the shaft size changes. If strength governs, d grows as T^(1/3), and T grows as 1/N. A shaft at one third the speed needs about 1.44 times the diameter for the same power. If stiffness governs, a long shaft may need to be larger still, because twist grows with length.

When two shafts are joined in series, the same torque passes through both and the twists add. When they are joined in parallel, the torques add and both twist by the same angle. That is covered in 6.4. Belt and gear drives themselves are machine-design topics; here we only need the power, torque and speed at the shaft.

figure.caption: For a fixed 10 kW, torque falls from about 955 N·m at 100 rpm to about 95 N·m at 1000 rpm. The curve is T = 60000P/(2πN).

spec.aria: Curve: for a fixed power of 10 kW, torque falls as shaft speed rises.

examples.question: An electric motor delivers 15 kW at 1440 rpm to a solid steel shaft. The allowable shear stress is 40 MPa. Find the minimum diameter. Choose a standard size from 20, 25, 30 and 35 mm.
steps: Strength limit for a solid shaft: τmax = 16T/(πd³). Rearrange: d³ = 16T/(πτallow).
The next standard size above 23.3 mm is 25 mm, so choose a 25 mm shaft.
examples.answer: The minimum diameter is 23.3 mm, so use a standard 25 mm shaft.
examples.check:
import math
P = 15000.0
N = 1440.0
tau = 40e6
omega = 2*math.pi*N/60
T = P/omega
d3 = 16*T/(math.pi*tau)
d = d3**(1/3)
print(round(T, 1))
print(round(d*1000, 1))

traps: Feeding rpm straight into P = Tω. Convert speed to rad/s first: ω = 2πN/60, with N in rpm.
Using kilowatts in P = Tω. Convert 15 kW to 15000 W before dividing by ω.
Mixing diameter and radius. The solid-shaft form τ = 16T/(πd³) uses the diameter throughout; J = πd⁴/32 also uses the diameter.
Rounding 23.3 mm down to 20 mm. A smaller shaft has higher shear stress, so always round up to the next standard size.
Passing the strength check and stopping. A long shaft can be strong enough yet twist too much; check θ/L = T/(GJ) from 6.2.

quiz.q: Define angular speed ω and write it in terms of N in rpm.
quiz.a: Angular speed is the angle turned per second, in rad/s. One turn is 2π rad and one minute is 60 s, so ω = 2πN/60.

quiz.q: Why does torque fall when speed rises at constant power?
quiz.a: P = Tω, so T = P/ω. For fixed P, torque is inversely proportional to angular speed. Doubling the speed halves the torque.

quiz.q: A shaft transmits 7.5 kW at 300 rpm. Find the torque.
The same shaft carries 238.7 N·m. The allowable shear stress is 50 MPa. Find the minimum solid diameter.
A shaft is designed for 10 kW at 1440 rpm. It is later run at 720 rpm delivering the same 10 kW. What happens to the torque and the maximum shear stress? Assume the same diameter.
quiz.a: T = P/ω, so halving the speed doubles the torque. Since τmax = 16T/(πd³), the shear stress also doubles. If the original design was at the allowable limit, the slower running is unsafe.

quiz.q: Two solid shafts of the same material transmit the same power, one at 500 rpm and one at 1500 rpm. If strength governs, compare their diameters.
Why is a stiffness check needed after the strength design?
quiz.a: Strength limits stress, while stiffness limits twist. A shaft can be strong enough yet twist so much that gears misalign or bearings load unevenly. Check θ/L = T/(GJ) against the allowable twist per unit length.

quiz.q: A 22 kW motor runs at 960 rpm. Find the torque using the kW form.

beyond: Not for the exam. In electric vehicles, the same relation sizes the motor-to-wheel drive: a single-speed reducer trades motor speed for wheel torque, and the shaft is checked for fatigue, not just static shear. Power plants use it to couple turbine and generator shafts, where torsional vibration and alignment matter more than static strength. Search for 'ASME shaft design', 'torsional vibration' and 'fatigue of shafts' to go further.
